extracted.intended_audience: readers of the Public Advertiser and the politically-engaged eighteenth-century public (citizens interested in government accountability)
extracted.subtask_description: Opinion/argumentative letters published in an 18th-century newspaper criticizing government, military conduct, and public figures, aimed at persuading the public and calling for accountability. Emphasizes factual inquiry, moral inference, and public reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing a nobleman's munificence
rubrics_metrics.description: "The proofs of his munificence must be drawn from the uses to which he has applied that fortune."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge a rich man's generosity by a single benevolent act; evaluate by sustained, public uses of his wealth (relief of indigence, encouragement of arts/science, protection of learning, rewards for genius). A solitary conspicuous act may prove little in an argument about overall character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferring motives from actions (internal evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: "We are to judge of the motives of men by the manifest tendency of their actions, nor by the notorious character of their minds... [not] only what could be proved in a court of justice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow internal and circumstantial evidence — the manifest tendency of actions and known temper — to inform judgments about public figures, not insisting solely on documentary proof or witness testimony. Some truths rest on internal evidence analogous to religious belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptive evidence from combination of facts and reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: "The evidence against the duke of Bedford is as strong as any presumptive evidence can be. It depends upon a combination of facts and reasoning, which require no confirmation from the anecdote..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A coherent combination of observed facts and logical inference can establish strong presumptive evidence even without direct documentary confirmation or anecdotal support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize frequency when forming complex generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the frequency of the fact which alone can make us comprehend how a man can be his own enemy... It is not a simple idea arising from a single fact, but a very complex idea arising from many facts, well observed, and accurately compared."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex characterizations (e.g., 'a man who is his own enemy') should be based on many observed instances rather than single occurrences; frequency and careful comparison are required to form reliable general ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid descending into petty verbal disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: "Junius will never descend to a dispute with such a writer... especially as the dispute must be chiefly about words... his time will always be more usefully employed than in the trifling refinements of verbal criticism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing public issues, focus on substantial facts and arguments rather than hair-splitting about wording or stylistic niceties; reserve verbal criticism when it materially affects the matter at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sarcasm from contradiction in rhetorical critique
rubrics_metrics.description: "Modestus cannot distinguish between a sarcasm and a contradiction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should correctly identify rhetorical devices (e.g., sarcasm, irony) rather than treating them as logical contradiction; misreading tone leads to unfair or weak rebuttals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate public officials by their subsequent conduct, not merely events beyond control
rubrics_metrics.description: "He lays no stress upon the event itself, as a ground of accusation against the ministry, but dwells entirely upon their subsequent conduct... He does not say that they are answerable for the offence, but for the scandalous neglect of their duty, in suffering an offence so flagrant to pass by without notice or inquiry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging ministers or officials, assess how they respond to incidents (investigation, prosecution, censure) rather than blaming them solely for unforeseeable events; failure to inquire or punish is itself culpable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold nature of military offences (legal vs. disciplinary)
rubrics_metrics.description: "They have committed two offences, both very enormous, and violated two laws. The rescue is one offence, the flagrant breach of discipline another; and hitherto it does not appear that they have been punished, or even censured for either."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between civil/common-law offences (e.g., rescuing a prisoner) and military offences (breach of discipline). Both layers warrant separate inquiry/punishment; immunity in one forum does not absolve the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate institutional remedies and the need for impartial inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: "Instead of ordering the officers concerned... to be put under arrest, and brought to trial, they would have it understood, that they did their duty completely... so that while the officers... escaped without censure, the poor men... are the only objects whom the ministry have thought proper to expose to punishment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper government response to scandal includes impartial investigation and, where warranted, courts-martial or trials of responsible officers. Superficial or selective punishment (targeting subordinates while protecting superiors) indicates malfeasance or ulterior motives and undermines public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political priority principle: major constitutional breaches overshadow lesser grievances
rubrics_metrics.description: "When the constitution is openly invaded... inferior grievances naturally lose their force, and are suffered to pass by without punishment or observation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public attention and activism naturally concentrate on fundamental constitutional threats; lesser abuses may be neglected in such periods, but this prioritization should not excuse ongoing ministerial abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: On rhetorical appeals to the public: appeal to understanding rather than inflaming passions
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have been accused of endeavouring to inflame the passions of the people. Let me now appeal to their understanding... He shall find me ready to maintain the truth of my narrative, and the justice of my observations upon it, at the hazard of my utmost credit with the public."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argumentation aimed at public persuasion should rely on factual narrative, reasoned commentary, and willingness to stake credibility rather than on mere emotional provocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing a military corps by collective spirit and discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: "Considering them as a corps, I fear, it will be found, that they are neither good soldiers nor good subjects... If these gentlemen were better soldiers, I am sure they would be better subjects."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate military units both for technical military competence and for their civic character; lapses in discipline or esprit de corps can indicate broader problems of subordination to civil authority and public duty.
